segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the System

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the great novels in the English language.

Over the course of this series, we'll be working our way through Charles Dickens's extraordinary anatomy of English life — the fog, the courts, the secrets, the suffering, and the astonishing humanity at the heart of it all.
I'm joined today by three guests whose different ways of reading this novel will, I hope, make it crackle back into life.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don, a critic in the great tradition, who believes that a novel's moral imagination matters far more than its social programme.
He reads Bleak House as a story about individual character under pressure — about goodness, self-sacrifice, and the frailty of the will.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows more about the actual institutions Dickens depicted than perhaps anyone now living.
He brings the real-world context — the law as it was, what poverty actually meant, and a dry wit that keeps the history honest.
And Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive.
He approaches every text as a performer first — he hears the rhythms, catches the comedy, and knows exactly when the silence should do the work.
We begin, as Dickens himself begins, with atmosphere — the fog, the ancient curse, the body on the bed.
What strikes me, before anything else, is that Dickens opens this novel with an act of extraordinary artistic confidence.
He does not begin with a character, or a plot, or even a scene in the conventional sense.
He begins with a condition — a moral and atmospheric condition — from which everything else will follow.
And the genius of that lies in the fact that the fog is not merely fog.
It is the outward form of a corruption that has settled so deep into English life that no one can quite see through it anymore.
Now, James will tell us what the Court of Chancery actually was — and I shall not quarrel with him on that.
But I would insist that Dickens is doing something more than institutional critique.
Edmund is entirely right that it is more than institutional critique — though the institutional critique is, I should note, also devastating and accurate.
But what interests me most, at the outset of this novel, is how quickly Dickens establishes that the corruption is not confined to the courts.
It runs through the great houses too — through the Dedlock family, through that long and terrible inheritance of pride.

There is a passage — a kind of origin myth for the Dedlock doom — in which a crippled ancestral lady, repudiating her husband on the very pavement where she has fallen, delivers something very close to a formal curse.

'I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!'
Now, that is Gothic machinery, certainly — but it is also a precise anatomy of how pride becomes hereditary fate.
The house is cursed not by magic, but by its own nature — and Dickens understood that perfectly.
What I find electrifying about that passage is the rhythm of it — the sheer repetition.
'I will walk here' — three times, each one heavier than the last — before that final command: 'let the Dedlocks listen for my step.'
When I read that aloud, I feel the weight of those words press down on everything that follows in the novel.
And Dickens earns every syllable of it — because he has shown us, in exquisite economy, this woman walking the terrace day after day, in sun and shadow, with greater difficulty every day.
She never complains. She never speaks of the pain. She simply endures — and then she curses.
Oliver puts his finger on something essential — and it connects, I think, to the larger question of sacrifice in this novel.
Dickens is endlessly fascinated by characters who make a terrible resolution and then live entirely inside it.
There is a passage — I know James has it — about Lady Dedlock's sister, and the letter she wrote to Boythorn, and what that letter cost her.
Yes — and it is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating passages in the novel.
Jarndyce is telling Esther about her mother's sister — who loved Boythorn, quarrelled with her sister, and then, in a single letter, erased herself.

'She wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did — and that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too.'
'In consideration for those master points in him, and even in consideration for them in herself, she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it.'
The syntax there is extraordinary — 'live in it and die in it' — as if the sacrifice were a room she locked herself into.
And the final line — 'certainly he never saw her, never heard of her from that hour. Nor did any one' — that last clause is almost unbearable in its brevity.
'Nor did any one.' Three words. Dickens knows exactly when to stop.
And the restraint is devastating precisely because everything before it has been so controlled, so carefully withheld.
When I read passages like that aloud, I find myself slowing almost to a full stop at the end — because the silence is the point.
The novel earns that silence. Everything that follows — all the secrets, all the shame — grows from that buried sacrifice.
And that buried world — the world of concealment and despair — has its most visceral expression not in the great houses but in the filthy room above Krook's shop.
The body of Nemo — the man who was everything and is now nothing — lying on a low bed in spectral candlelight.
Dickens describes that room with a kind of forensic disgust — every detail registered through Tulkinghorn's senses as he hesitates in the doorway.
'Through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.'
The lawyer's mouth. Not his nose, not his eyes — his mouth. As if the corruption is something you swallow.
That is not sentimentality about poverty. That is precision.
And it is a precision that serves the moral argument, which is what I would insist upon.
Nemo is not merely a victim of poverty — he is a man who has chosen annihilation.
The name itself — Nemo, no one — is a willed disappearance, not merely a social fact.
And that connects him, I think, to Lady Dedlock's sister — to all those characters in this novel who have, for one reason or another, chosen to die while living.
The fog, the curse, the body, the buried sacrifice — we are, even at this early stage, already deep inside the novel's central obsessions.
We'll be returning to all of these — the law, the secrets, the question of what it costs to live inside a resolution.
After the break, we turn to the Court of Chancery itself — the institution at the fog's heart — and what it actually meant to be caught inside it.

segments.title: Richard's Slow Descent: Ambition and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we read Dickens slowly enough to see what he's actually doing.
Today's deep dive concerns one of the novel's most quietly devastating portraits: Richard Carstone.
A young man who arrives in the novel full of charm and possibility, and whom we watch — chapter by chapter — squander both.
To examine how Dickens builds that arc, I'm joined as always by three remarkable readers.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, who reads Dickens as a moralist — and who will not let us forget that character is destiny.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who will tell us what Chancery was actually doing to real people in real time.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the man who has read more Dickens aloud than anyone — who hears the rhythms before he sees the argument.
Let's begin at the beginning of Richard's ruin — which is, rather beautifully, a scene of apparent hope.
What strikes me first, reading Chapter Thirteen carefully, is that Dickens frames Richard's problem not as poverty of circumstance but as poverty of will.
Esther — and Dickens always deploys Esther's moral intelligence precisely — observes this very clearly when the young couple confide in her.
She notes what the love will actually require — and her formulation is exacting.
That triad — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — is Dickens's moral vocabulary at its most classical.
Richard will prove congenitally unable to sustain any one of the three.

It comes to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake.
That triad — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — is Dickens's moral vocabulary at its most classical.
Richard will prove congenitally unable to sustain any one of the three.
Edmund is right — but I want to linger on what Esther says just before that.
She says: "They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That semi-colon is doing enormous work.
Esther is charmed by them, genuinely swept up — and then she catches herself and the narration pivots toward duty.
That pivot is where Dickens does his best work — in the gap between delight and responsibility.
Richard lives permanently on the delight side of that gap.
What Oliver is describing in literary terms has a concrete institutional dimension.
Richard is a ward in Chancery.
He has been raised in the expectation — never fulfilled, perpetually deferred — of an inheritance that the court is administering.
That structural position actively cultivates the habits Esther is trying to counsel against: deferral, dependence, the postponement of real effort.
Dickens understood this mechanism with great precision — Chancery doesn't merely delay justice, it distorts character.
And Jarndyce sees this coming — which makes his counsel to Richard in the same chapter all the more pointed.
Edmund, shall we hear what he actually says to the boy?
Jarndyce's address to Richard is one of the finest pieces of moral counsel in the novel — perhaps in Dickens entire.
It has the structure of a sermon without the sanctimony.
He opens by placing the young man before possibility — "the world is before you" — and then immediately grounds that vision in something unsparing.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
That image of the heathen waggoner — drawn from the fable of the man who prayed to Hercules without putting his shoulder to the wheel — is quintessential Dickens.
He takes a classical allusion and drives it, effortlessly, into plain English.
The passage builds, though — and the build is everything when you're reading it aloud.
Jarndyce moves from Providence to love to — and here is the sting — the ultimatum.

"If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
That rhythm — "ever was or could be, ever will or can be" — is not decorative.
It is Dickens pressing on the repetition until it becomes a kind of drum.
And the final clause — "leave your cousin Ada here" — lands like a verdict.
And yet Richard cannot hear it.
Jarndyce also offers him something quite remarkable — in the passage just before — a kind of unconditional pastoral care.
He tells them, and I find this extraordinarily generous for the period, that if they change their minds about each other, if love cools —
"Don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Jarndyce is dismantling the shame architecture that Victorian sentiment had built around love's failure.
That is a radically humane gesture — and Richard, typically, takes it as licence rather than as kindness.
James touches on something important there.
Jarndyce's great speech earlier in the chapter — when he speaks of having contemplated their union — is also careful to maintain distance.
That repeated "afar off" is doing very subtle moral work.
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility... But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
Jarndyce is not directing their futures — he is bearing witness, hoping, and withholding.
That restraint defines his entire moral authority in the novel.
Which brings us — and I think this is the passage I keep returning to — to what Esther sees as they leave.
Richard and Ada walk away through a sunlit room, and Esther watches, and Dickens lets himself be briefly — and I mean briefly — lyrical.
The writing slows and opens, and you feel the full cost of what is coming.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
"It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
He does not explain. He does not editorialize.
The weather does it. The architecture does it. And it is devastating.
And then we see, some chapters later, the institutional consequence of Richard's temperament made flesh — in the form of Mrs. Badger's assessment.
She is a comic character, certainly — but Dickens gives her a clinical precision that cuts.
She contrasts Richard directly with Allan Woodcourt, and the terms she uses are utterly specific.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
That is a portrait of vocation — the genuine article.
And Richard, by structural opposition, is its exact negative.
Mrs. Badger's phrase is remarkable — Richard has not "that positive interest" which "makes it his vocation."
The word "vocation" carries theological weight — a calling, in the old sense.
Richard is constitutionally unable to be called by anything except the siren song of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
And that, for Dickens, is not merely misfortune — it is moral failure.
I'd want to push back — gently — on calling it purely moral failure.
Dickens gives Richard's languidness a systemic cause.
He is, as Mrs. Badger says, of "such a very easy disposition that probably he would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels."
That ease is not wickedness — it is a particular kind of damage.
The suit has taught him that nothing is final, nothing requires full commitment — because tomorrow the court might rule in his favour.
It's a brilliant diagnosis — and Dickens makes it hurt precisely because Richard is not a villain but a victim of his own hope.
Victim of his own hope — I think that's the phrase that will stay with me from this conversation.
What Dickens has accomplished in these early chapters is to build the scaffold of a tragedy while disguising it as a romance.
The sun shines on Richard and Ada — and then the room darkens as they go out.
We'll be back shortly to follow that shadow further.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Shadow

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series in which we read Dickens's great novel slowly, carefully, and in excellent company.
Today's segment is called The Weight of Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Shadow.
We're deep in the machinery of the novel's central mystery — a secret buried in a Chancery document, a woman of high station, and a lawyer who knows too much.
With me today are three readers who bring very different lights to bear on this extraordinary novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and literary critic of the old school — for Edmund, the novel's greatness lies in moral imagination, in character tested by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions were, what it meant to be caught inside them, and why it still matters.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novels than anyone alive — hears every sentence as a performer first, and that instinct never fails him.
Let's begin with Mr. Tulkinghorn himself — that walking archive of other people's ruin.
Tulkinghorn is one of the great entrances in English fiction, and Dickens knows exactly what he's doing when he brings him across the terrace at Chesney Wold.
There's that wonderful line about his pace — it is never quickened, never slackened.
"He wears his usual expressionless mask — if it be a mask."
That parenthetical — if it be a mask — is doing extraordinary work.
Because Dickens is asking us: is this a man hiding behind a face, or is there simply nothing beneath the surface at all?
And then the clincher — he reads it as a performer would:
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every crease of his dress. That is a physical image of concealment I find quite unforgettable.
What strikes me is the precision of the moral paradox Dickens plants in the very next sentence.
He sets it up with almost lawyerly care, if you'll forgive the pun.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
Devotion or mercenary transaction — those are the only two possibilities, and we are told we shall never know which.
This is not social satire — this is a novelist asking the deepest question about a certain kind of man: is loyalty a virtue in him, or merely an instrument?
Dr. Johnson would have understood Tulkinghorn completely.
The historical irony, of course, is that Tulkinghorn is not unusual.
The great family solicitors of the nineteenth century occupied precisely that position — intimate with the affairs of the aristocracy, yet entirely excluded from their social world.
Which is exactly what Dickens catches in that phrase about Tulkinghorn being so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.
The power of those men came precisely from that anomaly — they could not be dismissed like servants, could not be ignored like tradespeople.
They knew where the bodies were buried — sometimes quite literally — and everyone in the house knew that they knew.
And when that knowledge is activated — when Tulkinghorn finally delivers his news — Dickens stages it as a piece of almost unbearable drawing-room theatre.
Sir Leicester fumbling with his eye-glass, misreading the letter, apologising for the delay — it's both comic and excruciating.
And then the message, read aloud by an oblivious husband to his terrified wife:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
I have seen him. Three words. Three words that could unravel a life.
And they are delivered by a man who has no idea what they mean to the woman sitting across from him.
The cruelty of that scene lies entirely in the dramatic irony, and Dickens is not in the least sentimental about it.
Sir Leicester is presented, throughout, as a man of genuine if limited dignity — he trusts his Lady absolutely, and that trust is itself part of his tragedy.
What interests me far more is what follows — the confrontation between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn, each watching the other from behind an impeccable social mask.
Dickens gives us their outward composure, and then opens a window onto what lies beneath it.

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
That construction — whether... whether... what — is a rhetorical triptych.
Each clause opens an abyss, and then Dickens closes the door on all of them with that single phrase: hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.
The phrase for the time is doing legal work there, whether Dickens intended it that way or not.
It implies a provisional settlement — a stay of proceedings — not a resolution.
And the extended passage describing their subsequent meetings makes that tension absolutely explicit.
"They meet again at dinner — again, next day — again, for many days in succession."
That repetition of again is the rhythm of surveillance — of two parties circling each other under the cover of social ceremony.
In legal terms you might call it a cold war — neither party willing to move first, both acutely aware that the first move may also be the last.
Lady Dedlock always the same exhausted deity — what a phrase that is.
Dickens writes her as a woman performing her own existence — terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
The shrine is her public self — her title, her beauty, her manner — and she is trapped inside it.
The secret doesn't just threaten to destroy her — it already has destroyed some essential freedom she might once have possessed.
That connects, I think, to the remarkable passage in which we learn how the arrangements around Esther Summerson were originally made.
Mr. Jarndyce tells Esther what little he was permitted to know of her origins — and the word permitted is exactly right.
"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt."
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
The steadfastness of her resolution — Dickens allows Lady Dedlock this at least: a fierce, ungovernable will, even in self-concealment.
She is not merely a victim of circumstance — she is an agent of her own concealment, however terrible the cost.
And that assumed name — she tells Kenge that her name is an assumed one — is historically very resonant.
Women in her situation — women with illegitimate children, women who had crossed the rigid lines of Victorian moral respectability — had very few instruments of self-protection.
An assumed name was one of them — a legal fiction deployed in the service of social survival.
Tulkinghorn, of course, understands this perfectly — which is precisely what makes him so dangerous.
He is not merely a keeper of secrets — he is a man who understands the exact price of every one of them.
What's remarkable, I think, is how Dickens sustains this atmosphere across so many chapters — the watching, the silence, the mutual awareness — without any of it ever becoming melodrama.
Edmund, Oliver, James — thank you.
In our next segment, we turn to Esther Summerson herself — narrator, orphan, and perhaps the most quietly radical creation in the entire novel.

segments.title: Laughter and Paradox in the Court of Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracing the fog and the misery of Chancery — but Dickens is also one of the supreme comic writers in the language, and today we're looking at how laughter operates inside this great novel.
How does he make us laugh at things that are, on closer inspection, genuinely terrible?
To dig into that, I'm joined as ever by our three experts.

Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a great moral story about character under pressure — and who is not always persuaded that satire improves on straightforward ethical judgement.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who knows exactly what these institutions actually were and what it cost real people to be caught inside them.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone living — who hears the comic timing in every sentence and can tell us when the laughter is doing something darker than it first appears.
Oliver, you've been itching to talk about Lady Dedlock and her world — and specifically about the extraordinary passage in chapter two where Dickens turns her entire social position inside out.
Over to you.
The thing that knocks me flat every time I read this passage is that Dickens constructs the joke with absolute architectural precision.
Lady Dedlock believes herself — and here I want to use Dickens's own words — quote, an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
She sees herself in her glass, where indeed she looks so.
That little parenthetical — where indeed she looks so — is devastating, because it grants her the beauty while stripping her of the power.
And then the machinery of the joke is revealed: every single person orbiting her — from her maid to the opera manager — has taken an exact moral inventory of her weaknesses.
They nurse her, they flatter her, and they lead her wherever they please.
And then comes the image that makes the whole thing soar.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
Lady Dedlock is the fleet.
Magnificent, immovable, and being towed away by a man turning her round his finger.
I think Oliver is right about the comic mechanism, and I don't want to resist the pleasure of it.
But I would observe that what Dickens is also doing — with perfect moral seriousness beneath the comedy — is diagnosing a particular kind of vanity.
Lady Dedlock has mistaken her position in the world for her nature.
That is a very old error, and a very costly one — as the novel will demonstrate in full.
The jewellers and the librarian who manage her are not, in themselves, villains.
Dickens even tells us that Mr. Sladdery, who says he can turn them round his finger — does not exaggerate at all.
He is, we are told, an honest man.
The comedy resides entirely in her self-deception, not in their manipulation.
Both points well made — but I'd want to add the institutional dimension, because what Dickens has captured here is something a social historian finds genuinely remarkable.
The mid-Victorian luxury trade was organised precisely around the exploitation of aristocratic vanity.
Blaze and Sparkle — Sheen and Gloss — these names are not simply comic invention.
They describe a real class of merchant whose entire business model depended on controlling access to fashionable reputation.
Lady Dedlock thinks she confers prestige on the shop; the shop has spent years engineering the circumstances under which she believes that.
And Dickens sees this with the eye of an economist as much as a satirist.
And from the very tip of the social pyramid, Dickens plunges us down into Chancery — where the comedy turns considerably darker.
There is this extraordinary moment in chapter three — a woman, an old woman, a former ward of Chancery, encountered by Esther and her companions.
Richard has called her mad — he's a young man, well-meaning, nervous — and she turns on him instantly.
She says — and this is the speech I find almost unbearable to read aloud because of the way it keeps curtsying at you as it destroys itself —
"I was a ward myself. I was not mad at that time. I had youth and hope. I believe, beauty. It matters very little now."
And then, with perfect deadpan ferocity —
"Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
Those short sentences — each one a life reduced to a phrase — are among the most brilliant pieces of dark comedy in the English novel.
I want to resist the word comedy there — not because Oliver is wrong about the technique, but because the passage functions primarily as a lament.
Youth, hope, beauty — three gifts, all squandered not by the woman herself, but by the system that held her.
And her identification of the sixth seal with the Great Seal of Chancery — that is not comic invention, that is the logic of a mind that has spent decades watching one institution devour everything.
Where Oliver hears Dickens the entertainer, I hear Dickens the moralist — and I think here they happen to be the same voice.
The phrase 'I expect a judgment shortly' would have landed with particular force on any reader who knew what Chancery actually was.
Judgments in Chancery were not shortly.
Cases ran for decades — for generations.
The woman's expectation of a judgment has already collapsed into an eschatological joke — she will wait for the Day of Judgment, because Chancery is functionally the same thing.
It's very dark, and it's very precise, and it would have been recognised immediately as precise by Dickens's original audience.
Let me bring in the Snagsby passage, because it's a different flavour entirely — pure Gothic comedy, and I find it almost impossible to read without laughing and feeling slightly watched.
Mr. Snagsby is a timid man enmeshed in secrets he barely understands, and his wife has become his permanent supernatural observer.
Listen to how Dickens closes the chapter —
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."

"And into whatsoever atmosphere of secrecy his own shadow may pass, let all concerned in the secrecy beware! For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
The Biblical register — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh — turned into a threat.
The marriage vow become a surveillance operation.
That inversion of the Book of Genesis is not accidental — it never is with Dickens.
He takes the language of sacred covenant and reassigns it to domestic tyranny.
The comedy is real — the image of Mrs. Snagsby as a frilled and night-capped ghost is genuinely absurd — but the subject is the prison of marriage when trust has collapsed entirely.
Dickens permits us the laugh, but he does not permit us to forget what the laugh is covering.
And I would note that the Snagsby marriage operates as a microcosm of the wider surveillance culture that runs through the novel.
Tulkinghorn watches Lady Dedlock; Bucket watches everyone; Mrs. Snagsby watches Snagsby.
The novel is saturated with people whose primary activity is observation — gathering intelligence to be used, eventually, as leverage.
Mrs. Snagsby is comic because she is wrong about what she is watching — but she is doing exactly what the institution of Chancery itself does: following, recording, waiting.
Which brings me to perhaps the most purely funny moment in our selection today — Mr. Smallweed, Mr. Bucket, and the singed will.
By this point in the novel we've been through tragedy after tragedy, and then Dickens gives us this — Bucket's whispered aside to Jarndyce about the Smallweed family's internal politics.
I have to read it, because no summary does it justice.
"Hadn't settled how to make their market of it. Quarrelled and hinted about it. I laid out twenty pound upon it."
"First the avaricious grandchildren split upon him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably long, and then they split on one another."
"Lord! There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
Too weak in her mind to drive a bargain — that is the single funniest exemption clause in Victorian fiction.
Bucket's delivery — that whispered aside, that conspiratorial 'Lord!' — is the voice of a man who has spent his entire career watching human nature at its most transactional.

And what he's describing is a real legal phenomenon — documents with potential value becoming objects of family warfare, withheld, bargained over, half-destroyed in botched attempts to suppress or leverage them.
The paper itself is stained and singed — thrown on a fire and hastily snatched off again — which tells you all you need to know about how many minds have changed about what to do with it.
And the comedy is inseparable from the pathos, because this burnt document is the thing that could have ended Jarndyce and Jarndyce — and ended the suffering of everyone trapped inside it.
Bucket himself is a remarkable creation precisely because he finds humanity genuinely amusing without ceasing to be moral.
He has seen every variety of human weakness — greed, vanity, fear, sentimentality — and he is not contemptuous, but neither is he deceived.
That conjunction of clear sight and good humour is, I think, one of Dickens's own most characteristic qualities — and Bucket is the character in whom it is most fully embodied.
What strikes me, listening to all of this, is how consistently the laughter in Bleak House is laughter at a system — not laughter that excuses it.

Lady Dedlock is managed by her tradespeople; the old ward in Chancery waits for the Day of Judgment; Mrs. Snagsby shadows her husband through the night; and the Smallweed family would sell one another for two pounds.
All of it funny — and all of it damning.

In our next segment, we'll be turning to one of the novel's most discussed technical achievements — Dickens's use of two narrative voices — and asking what is at stake in giving half the novel to Esther Summerson.

segments.title: Jo's Testimony: The Voice of the Outcast

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're deep inside one of the novel's most extraordinary chapters — the inquest into the death of the man called Nemo.
It's a chapter that gathers together some of Dickens's most devastating social writing — and some of his funniest.
With us today are three guests who bring very different lenses to this material.
Sir Edmund Leigh — the Oxford critic who believes the novel's greatness lives in its moral imagination, not its polemics.
Professor James Blackstone — legal and social historian, for whom the institutions in this chapter are not metaphor but lived reality.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook narrator, and the man who hears Dickens's prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Let's begin with Nemo's death — with the terrible vacancy it reveals.
What strikes me first about this chapter is what the coroner's inquest is actually designed to establish — and how comprehensively it fails.
An inquest exists to determine identity, cause of death, and social connection — to place a body within a network of obligation.
Nemo has none of those things. Forty-five years of life and nothing — no record, no traceable thread.
Dickens puts it with an image that I find genuinely haunting.
The lonely figure on the bed lies there with no more track behind him that any one can trace than a deserted infant.
A deserted infant — which is to say, a person who has lived nearly half a century and arrived at death with less social substance than a newborn.
That is what absolute poverty and isolation do to a human being, in the world this novel describes.
James is right about the power of that image, though I'd want to situate it slightly differently.
The image of the deserted infant is not primarily sociological — it is theological.
The deserted infant is a figure of absolute vulnerability before Providence — which is precisely the condition in which Nemo dies.
Dickens is not merely indicting society here. He is posing a question about what the soul owes to the human community, and what the human community owes in return.
And the answer the chapter gives — through Jo — is quite remarkable.
Before we get to Jo, can we just spend a moment with Mrs. Piper?
Because Dickens gives us this entire chapter of genuine tragedy, and then drops Mrs. Piper into the middle of it like a depth charge of comic genius.
She has, Dickens tells us, a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell.
That single sentence is a complete portrait — and a complete critique of the inquest — delivered in twenty words.
And then she proceeds to prove it — at enormous length, while worrying about Johnny's head and whether Mrs. Perkins might be brought forward.
What I love — as a performer — is that all of Mrs. Piper's testimony is entirely useless, and Dickens makes you feel that the inquest deserves no better.
Oliver's absolutely right that Mrs. Piper is comic — but there's a very bitter point underneath the comedy.
In a functioning legal proceeding, witnesses are sworn, testimony is tested, evidence is weighed.
What this inquest produces instead is neighbourhood gossip, rumour, and fear of a dead man's facial expression.
And then Jo arrives — and the proceeding shows its true character by excluding him entirely.
The testimony of Jo is, I think, one of the most considered passages Dickens ever wrote — and one of the most carefully constructed.
Listen to the rhythm of it — the way Dickens strips language down to its absolute minimum to mirror Jo's own condition.
No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school.
Four short declarative negations. Each one a door closing.
And then, immediately, this extraordinary sentence — Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie.
Jo has no education, no family, no theology — and yet he possesses a moral sense that the proceedings around him conspicuously lack.
When I've read that passage aloud, I've had to slow down almost to a stop on those four short sentences.
Because each one is a complete world of deprivation compressed into four or five words.
And then Dickens does something astonishing — he has Jo defend himself to the court with the only moral vocabulary he has.

Can't exactly say what'll be done to him arter he's dead if he tells a lie to the gentlemen here, but believes it'll be something wery bad to punish him, and serve him right — and so he'll tell the truth.
He doesn't know doctrine. He doesn't know scripture. He knows that lying is wrong and that he'll answer for it.
And the court throws him out anyway.
And it's at that point that the narrator steps in — directly, in his own voice — to address Jo personally.
It's one of the most unusual moments in the novel — Dickens abandoning the fiction entirely to speak to his own character.
That intrusion of the narrator's voice is something I find both powerful and — I confess — slightly dangerous.
When Dickens addresses Jo directly — Jo, is it thou? — he is reaching past the story to claim a kind of moral authority over the reader's response.
And one might resist that — except that what follows is so tender, and so precise, that the resistance dissolves.
He calls Jo a rejected witness, and then says he is not quite in outer darkness.
There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'
The mispronunciation — wery — is not mocked. It is cherished. That is the precision I mean.
That line — He wos wery good to me, he wos — I have never found a way to read it aloud without feeling it.
Dickens gives Jo the most inarticulate possible reason for grief — a single repeated affirmation of simple goodness received — and it devastates.
Edmund called it a distant ray of light. But in the context of everything else in this chapter — all that darkness — it burns.
I want to follow that ray of light, if I may, into a very different part of the novel — because the law's treatment of Jo at this inquest is not an aberration.
It is precisely how the system is designed to operate — and Dickens, later in the novel, gives us the clearest possible anatomy of that design.
The scene with Mr. Kenge defending Mr. Vholes against any possible reform is one of the funniest — and most accurately observed — passages of legal satire in the English language.
Kenge says, quite without embarrassment — Repeal this statute, my dear sir? Never, with my consent.
Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth.

And then the parliamentary inquiry — five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine questions — which is killed stone dead by the answer: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a most respectable man.
That is not satire that exaggerates. That is satire that reports.
James, I take your point about the Kenge passage — it is brilliantly done.
But I'd distinguish between Dickens the satirist and Dickens the novelist. The satire targets institutions. The novel — at its deepest level — is about people.
And the passage that moves me most in all of this is not Kenge's parliamentary comedy — it is Mrs. Rouncewell pleading for her son.
She says something to Lady Dedlock that cuts straight through all the class and institutional armour around them both.

My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves.
That plea — pray, oh, pray — is not rhetoric. It is a mother on her knees, in language.
The doubling — pray, oh, pray — is something you only truly hear when you read it aloud. On the page it looks merely emphatic.
In the voice, it breaks. The oh is where the composure goes.
Dickens describes Mrs. Rouncewell as pleading with genuine simplicity — and that phrase is a stage direction as much as a narrative observation.
She is the same figure as Jo, in a sense — someone who has no power in the formal structures of the world, appealing on the basis of love alone.
Oliver's comparison is apt, and I think it extends further.

Jo before the coroner, Mrs. Rouncewell before Lady Dedlock, the laity before Mr. Kenge — they are all in the same structural position: appealing to a system that has arranged itself to be impervious to appeal.
What Dickens understood — and what makes the novel still feel contemporary — is that institutional respectability is itself a form of violence.
That phrase — institutional respectability as a form of violence — feels like the thread that runs through everything we've discussed today.
Jo rejected at the inquest. The law defended by Mr. Vholes's reputation. Mrs. Rouncewell asking for justice that the structure of her world makes almost impossible to deliver.
And yet Dickens never lets us forget that distant ray of light — the simple fact that Nemo was very good to Jo, and that Jo remembered it.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan.
We'll be back with another chapter of Bleak House Unpacked very soon.

segments.title: The Machinery of Fate: Dickens and Technique

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the programme that takes one of the greatest and most ferociously constructed novels in the English language and asks what it's actually doing.
I'm your host, and today we open with the machinery itself — Dickens's technique, the devices he uses to build a world so dense and strange it feels less like fiction than weather.
Joining me are three voices I'm genuinely delighted to have around this table.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, defender of the novel as moral imagination, and a man who believes atmosphere serves character, not thesis.
Professor James Blackstone — legal and social historian, who can tell you exactly what the Court of Chancery was, what it cost, and what it destroyed.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the most experienced reader of Dickens aloud that I know of, who hears the rhythms of this prose as few readers ever do.
Let's begin at the very beginning — because the opening of Bleak House is, I think, one of the most remarkable first pages in all of English fiction.
It opens without a verb.
"London." Full stop.
That single word is an indictment, a weather forecast, and a death sentence, all at once.
And then Dickens builds this extraordinary crescendo of noun phrases — fog, mud, dogs, horses, foot passengers — none of them quite alive, all of them afflicted.
Then, right in the middle of this primordial gloom, he drops the most extraordinary sentence.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur. Waddling up Holborn Hill. The man is sublime.
What's easy to miss, if you're reading for the comedy, is how historically precise that image is.
The eighteen-fifties were the decade of geological sensation — the Crystal Palace dinosaurs had just been unveiled, Mantell and Owen were fighting over prehistoric taxonomy.
Dickens places his readers on the cusp of a world that doesn't know its own age, that can't measure time with any confidence.
And Chancery, of course, is the perfect emblem of that — a legal system so ancient and encrusted that it has lost all memory of its original purpose.
The mud accumulates, as Dickens puts it, "at compound interest."
That is not a decorative phrase. That is how Chancery worked.
I want to resist the temptation — and I feel it is a temptation — to reduce that opening to a pamphlet against legal reform.
What Dickens achieves technically is something far more uncanny than polemic.
He gives us a world that has arrested itself — where daylight is provisional, where the sun is in mourning, where dogs and horses and men are equally undistinguishable in mire.
The moral imagination at work there is essentially tragic, not satirical.
It says: this is what happens when a civilisation loses the capacity to judge, to decide, to act.
The fog is not a metaphor for capitalism. It is a portrait of moral paralysis.
I think Edmund is right — and I think the proof of it is how Dickens handles his grotesques when the satire turns genuinely savage.
Take Boythorn — glorious, thundering, absurd Boythorn — and his war with Sir Leicester over a right of way.
This is comic writing of the very highest order, but it has an edge as sharp as a dropped gate.
Listen to the rhythm when he gets into full flood.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That triple "Ha, ha, ha" — written into the prose — is a stage direction. Dickens is telling the reader exactly where to laugh, and for how long.
The symmetry of those parallel clauses — "he brings, I bring, he brings, I defend" — is the symmetry of law itself turned to farce.
The comedy is real, but the mechanics beneath it are entirely accurate.
Right-of-way disputes between landowners and their neighbours were ruinously expensive and essentially interminable in the mid-Victorian courts.
Boythorn is wealthy enough to sustain the battle indefinitely, and that is precisely the joke — only the rich can afford the luxury of principle.
Meanwhile Richard Carstone, who cannot afford to sustain anything, is consumed by a suit he can neither win nor abandon.
Dickens knew exactly what he was doing in placing these two portraits side by side.
The Richard Carstone portrait is where I think Dickens's technique becomes genuinely formidable — and where the case for moral imagination, rather than social critique, is strongest.
Enter Vholes — and if ever a character were conjured purely through the sound of language, it is he.
Every sentence Vholes speaks is a small legal instrument, perfectly formed, utterly hollow.
Dickens gives him this extraordinary speech to Esther — all professional duty and open dealing — and the technique is to let the language condemn itself.
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
"I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
"Charged to no one" — in a novel obsessed with costs that can never be recovered, that phrase is devastating.
Vholes devours Richard in the name of duty, and never raises his voice once.
There is a moment of technique in this novel that I find almost unbearably good — and it's quieter than anything we've discussed.
George Rouncewell, alone in Chesney Wold in those terrible late chapters, moving through the empty rooms with a lamp.
Dickens piles up what he's thinking of — the murdered Tulkinghorn, the vanished Lady Dedlock, Sir Leicester broken upstairs — and then arrives at this.
"He looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy."
"But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
That repetition of "blank" — he does it twice — is not carelessness. That is a knell.
The novel has been building towards absence, and here Dickens names it. Not horror. Blankness.
That passage speaks to something Burke understood — that the truly terrible is not the spectacular but the silent withdrawal of meaning.
George Rouncewell is a soldier — a man formed by action, by the physical world — and he is confronted with a house that refuses to give him anything to do.
There is no ghost. There is no one to fight. There is only the blank.
That, I would argue, is Dickens operating at the very summit of his powers — not as a reformer, but as a tragedian.
I won't argue with tragedian. But I'd note that the blankness has a very specific social address.
Chesney Wold emptied. The great house — the seat of Dedlock power, of aristocratic continuity — reduced to a soldier holding up a lamp in the dark.
Dickens is not indifferent to what that represents as a historical fact, as well as a personal tragedy.
An entire order of society — sealed in fog, accumulated in mud, consumed by its own legal processes — going dark, room by room.
Fog, mud, dinosaurs, a fire engine deployed against a one-eyed villain, and a room that offers the trooper only blankness.
What strikes me listening to all three of you is that the technique and the feeling are inseparable in this novel — the form is the argument.
We're going to stay with that idea — the form as argument — as we turn next to the characters who are themselves destroyed by the machinery we've been describing.

segments.title: Closing: The Fog Lifts, but the Stain Remains

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through some of the darkest and most luminous passages Dickens ever wrote.
Before we close, I want to ask each of you: what stays with you — what is the residue of Bleak House once the fog has lifted?
Edmund, you've been our conscience in some ways today — let's begin with you.
What stays with me is the brickmaker's speech — which is, in its own way, one of the most morally devastating passages in the English novel.
Dickens gives that man — that brutal, drunken, violent man — something extraordinarily rare in Victorian fiction: rhetorical sovereignty.
He pre-empts every charitable question before it can be asked, and answers it with searing, unsparing honesty.
He says, in so many words:
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!"
That isn't self-pity. That is argument. Ferocious, dignified argument addressed to the complacency of the well-meaning.
Dickens understood that poverty does not ennoble — it degrades and brutalises — and he had the honesty to show it without flinching.
And yet, by the novel's end, he offers us Sir Leicester — broken, half-paralysed, his world in ruins — and something rather extraordinary happens.
The narrator says of his fidelity and his generous conquest of his own pride:
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
The brickmaker and the baronet: both children of the dust.
Edmund has put his finger on something I find essential about this novel's lasting power.

The brickmaker's speech is, institutionally speaking, a precise indictment of what we might now call the poverty of charitable intervention — the assumption that a tract and a home visit can substitute for clean water and living wages.
He doesn't merely reject Mrs. Pardiggle's charity — he exposes the entire logic of it.
And then there is Jo — that graceless creature, as the narrator calls him, with devastating precision.
What haunts me is the simple detail of what Nemo did for him on a cold winter night.
He came back, and having questioned him and found that he had not a friend in the world, said:
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
That small transaction — two friendless people briefly acknowledging each other — is what Dickens sets against all the machinery of law, charity, and class.
It is not enough. It was never enough. But it is all either of them had.
James has made me want to weep, which I consider entirely appropriate.
What I carry away from this novel — every time, without exception — is the sheer strangeness of Tulkinghorn.
Because Dickens fills this book with suffering that has a face, a name, a voice — and then places at its centre a man who is simply a shell.
The narrator is absolutely precise about it:
"He has shown neither patience nor impatience, nor attention nor abstraction. He has shown nothing but his shell."
And then that extraordinary simile — listen to this:
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
That sentence is a piece of music in itself — the word 'case' doing double duty with such gorgeous economy.
Dickens builds this entire novel on that contrast: the suffering that overflows into every sentence, and the emptiness at the heart of power that cannot feel it.
The fog lifts, as your title has it — but Tulkinghorn's case never opens. That is the stain that remains.
Oliver has said something I want to press on just slightly.
The emptiness at the heart of power — yes, absolutely.
But Dickens is careful not to make that the only word on the powerful.
Sir Leicester is powerful — absurd in many ways, rigid in his class prejudices — and yet Dickens insists on his moral redemption.
His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant shielding of her — these are the narrator's words, and they are not ironic.
Tulkinghorn is the shell. Sir Leicester is the instrument that, after terrible damage, finally makes its music heard.
A shell and an instrument — I think that may be the finest note on which to close.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation of quite exceptional richness.
Bleak House rewards every return — and I hope today has sent you back to it, or towards it for the first time.
This has been Bleak House Unpacked. Thank you for listening.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may

everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.

most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by

a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should

living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the

length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell

blank as the oppressive silence.

and for us besides. Have I read the little book wot you left? No, I
an’t read the little book wot you left. There an’t nobody here as
knows how to read it; and if there wos, it wouldn’t be suitable to
me. It’s a book fit for a babby, and I’m not a babby. If you was to
leave me a doll, I shouldn’t nuss it. How have I been conducting of
myself? Why, I’ve been drunk for three days; and I’da been drunk four
if I’da had the money. Don’t I never mean for to go to church? No, I
don’t never mean for to go to church. I shouldn’t be expected there,
if I did; the beadle’s too gen-teel for me. And how did my wife get
that black eye? Why, I give it her; and if she says I didn’t, she’s a
Lie!”
c8:p88.summary: The brickmaker delivers a searing response, preempting Mrs. Pardiggle's usual questions by cataloguing his poverty, his drinking, his family's deaths, his wife's bruise from his own violence, and the futility of charitable intervention.
c8:p88.best_quote: Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead! An't my place dirty? Yes, it is dirty—it's nat'rally dirty, and it's nat'rally onwholesome; and we've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides.

c58:p70.text:
His formal array of words might have at any other time, as it has
often had, something ludicrous in it, but at this time it is serious
and affecting. His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant
shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own
pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true. Nothing
less worthy can be seen through the lustre of such qualities in the
commonest mechanic, nothing less worthy can be seen in the best-born
gentleman. In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both
children of the dust shine equally.
c58:p70.summary: The narrator reflects that Sir Leicester's earnestness, fidelity, and generous conquering of his own pride for Lady Dedlock's sake transcend class and honor all humanity.
c58:p70.best_quote: "In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."

c11:p87.text:
That graceless creature only knows that the dead man (whom he
recognized just now by his yellow face and black hair) was sometimes
hooted and pursued about the streets. That one cold winter night when
he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man
turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and
found that he had not a friend in the world, said, “Neither have I.
Not one!” and gave him the price of a supper and a night’s lodging.
That the man had often spoken to him since and asked him whether he
slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man
had no money, he would say in passing, “I am as poor as you to-day,
Jo,” but that when he had any, he had always (as the boy most
heartily believes) been glad to give him some.
c11:p87.summary: Jo reveals the dead man recognized him, showed him kindness, asked about his welfare, and when poor himself, shared what little he had.
c11:p87.best_quote: Neither have I. Not one! and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.

c11:p33.text:
During this dialogue Mr. Tulkinghorn has stood aloof by the old
portmanteau, with his hands behind him, equally removed, to all
appearance, from all three kinds of interest exhibited near the
bed—from the young surgeon’s professional interest in death,
noticeable as being quite apart from his remarks on the deceased as
an individual; from the old man’s unction; and the little crazy
woman’s awe. His imperturbable face has been as inexpressive as his
rusty clothes. One could not even say he has been thinking all this
while. He has shown neither patience nor impatience, nor attention
nor abstraction. He has shown nothing but his shell. As easily might
the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case,
as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case.
c11:p33.summary: Extended description of Tulkinghorn's complete emotional and physical detachment, his mysterious positioning by the portmanteau, and his unreadable nature.
c11:p33.best_quote: As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case.
